dimensions.note: applicationKey is .meta({ sensitive: true }) and documented as vault-sourced; it is never echoed into a payload, a snapshot or a log line. The 24h authorizationToken is treated as the bearer credential it is: sent only in the Authorization header, never persisted. Asserted by execution, not by reading — 'no method leaks a secret into a snapshot or a log line' drives all six methods and greps every write and log for both secrets, and 'the bearer token is sent as a header and never as a body field' checks every non-authorize request. The mechanical harness repeats the credential grep independently across all eight observed writes (step 5, OK). B2 never returns SSE-C key material, so no file payload can carry one. Residual, documented rather than fixed: fileInfo is arbitrary user metadata that B2 stores with each file and returns on every read, so it lands in a snapshot verbatim — the README warns it must never hold a credential, matching the bucketInfo precedent in @sntxrr/b2/bucket.

Structured throughout: message templates with named placeholders and a props object, never string concatenation of values. Warnings are reserved for facts an operator must not miss and each names the consequence rather than the symptom — truncation says the counts are a FLOOR, hide says the data underneath is still stored and billed, non-current bytes name the lifecycle rule that would reap them, and a requested-but-invisible bucket is warned rather than skipped silently. The truncation warning earned its keep in production: on the first live fleet scan the default maxPages of 50 capped the six largest buckets, and it was the truncated flag — not the byte total, which looked plausible — that revealed the first answer was a floor. One defect found and fixed during review: update accepted bypassGovernance alongside a legal-hold-only change and dropped it silently, which would leave an operator believing a governance lock had been overridden when nothing was attempted; it now warns, covered by a test.

b2Fetch throws Error & { status, b2Code } and the model branches on the code, never on message text. 401 unauthorized is deliberately not retried — a missing capability is not transient, and the README maps each method to the capabilities it needs so the fix is the key's grant. Guards throw sentences that state what was refused and how to proceed, not assertion failures. Ordering was audited: every gate (destruction, compliance, detailed-mode prefix/maxFiles, REPLACE-without-contentType) fires before any B2 call, asserted by tests that check calls.length === 0. One real ordering defect was found and fixed: copy resolved the destination bucket's NAME after the copy had already landed, so a lookup failure would have stranded a completed side effect behind a failed method. Re-verified in the current source at b2_files.ts:2004-2023 — destinationName is resolved, and an unresolvable ID throws, before the payload is assembled — and locked in by 'copy refuses an unresolvable destination BEFORE copying anything', which asserts b2_copy_file was never issued.

87 tests, all mocked, plus a mechanical harness (ALL PASS). Everything the previous review recorded still holds. What it did NOT catch is the point of this version: the removed pre-flight check had a test, and that test asserted the broken behaviour was correct — it drove the check directly with globalArgs and asserted it blocks without allowFileDestruction and passes with it, both of which are true and neither of which is the property that matters. The suite therefore ENCODED the bug rather than catching it, exactly as the wave-1 unprunedPrefixes test did. A test written from the same mental model as the code cannot falsify that model; only running the thing can, and running it is what exposed this. The replacement asserts the property instead of the implementation: every check that applies to delete must PASS on a well-configured model that has not pre-authorised destruction, so the per-run acknowledgement can reach execute at all. Treating an absent appliesTo as 'applies to delete' is deliberate, since a check that omits it runs everywhere. Verified to bite by reintroducing the deleted check verbatim and confirming the new test fails, then removing it again and confirming green.

scan and sync are read-only and naturally repeatable. delete is idempotent per CONVENTIONS §3: a 404, or a 400 with b2Code file_not_present or no_such_file, is a success that still writes the exists=false tombstone, and a name that resolves to nothing skips the call entirely. isAlreadyGone deliberately excludes bad_bucket_id — that is a configuration bug, and swallowing it would report a successful delete of a file still sitting in the bucket the caller meant; asserted directly. reauth is threaded through every call site so a long fleet drain survives the 24h token expiring mid-scan; the live 2.7M-version scan exercised that path for real. hide and copy are not idempotent by nature (each writes a new version) and are documented as such rather than pretending otherwise.

Built against the v4 corrections in CONVENTIONS §4 rather than Backblaze's own prose. The canonical client (§5) was verified byte-identical to b2-account, b2-bucket and b2-key by diff after formatting, so no local drift was introduced. LIVE-VERIFIED 2026-08-05 against the real account — a full fleet scan across every bucket, 2,693,460 versions and 39.49 GiB of non-current data — which is the gate the previous draft of this report could only flag as pending. Per PRD §7 item 3 that run beat all 86 mock tests, and found three contract-level defects, all now fixed and tested: (1) B2 omits legalHold and fileRetention ENTIRELY from a list response on a bucket without Object Lock, so a zero legalHoldOnCount meant 'not reported', not 'not locked' — unwrapAuthorized already separated unreadable (false) from readable, but absent (null) had no accounting, and lockFieldsAbsentCount now carries it; (2) sync, delete and update forced a bucket-ID lookup their B2 calls never need when addressed by fileId, locking out a bucket-restricted key that lacks listBuckets; (3) the copy ordering defect recorded under error-handling. The authorization-wrapper trap (§4.3) is handled generically by unwrapAuthorized. The slim-response trap is handled: b2_update_file_legal_hold and b2_update_file_retention return only the id, name and changed field, so update re-reads via the class-B b2_get_file_info rather than snapshotting a hollowed-out body; asserted. defaultRetention/fileRetention is modelled as an object, not a string (§4.6). Residual: the four nested-blob element shapes remain unmodelled pending observation of a non-empty instance in the wild.

Two specs, cleanly separated by what they describe: aggregate is per-bucket/per-prefix inventory (30 schema fields), file is one immutable file VERSION (23). scan is a genuine factory — one execution fans out across every bucket the key can see and acquires the per-model lock once, rather than N contending runs (CLAUDE.md rule 6); the live fleet run confirmed that shape holds at 24 buckets. Cost is designed against and reported, not hidden: class-C transactions are counted honestly (one per 1000 files, so a 10000-file page bills as ten), the default page size is the B2 maximum because it costs the same as ten small pages while making a tenth of the round trips, and detailed mode stops listing once maxFiles is in hand so it does not pay to enumerate a million versions and discard all but a thousand. Aggregate mode is the default precisely because per-file emission over a restic repo would write tens of thousands of snapshots. Known operational limit, not a code defect: the default maxPages of 50 truncates buckets past roughly 500k versions, so any consumer scheduling this model must raise it or read truncated before reading a byte total.

Every fixture and README example uses example.com-class names and fake-but-plausible B2 identifiers (example-backup-bucket, 4a48fe8875c6214145260818, a1b2c3d4e5f6, K004example...). No real bucket name, account ID, key ID or homelab hostname appears in the model, the tests, the README or the mechanical harness — re-checked after the live run, which is exactly when real bucket names tend to leak into a fixture or a comment; the mechanical harness's own output names only example-backup-bucket. The only real-world specifics are the restic path conventions (data/, index/, snapshots/), which are public properties of restic's on-disk format, not of this account.

Deliberately calibrated per CONVENTIONS §4.9 — permissive where the shape is unobserved, strict where it is documented and observed. Byte and count fields are z.number().int() because B2 documents contentLength as an integer and a non-integer there would be a genuine contract change worth failing on; that trade-off is adjudicated, not accidental. The honest-null contract is enforced in the schema itself: every version-derived metric is .nullable() and the descriptions say null means 'not measured', never zero. The live run extended that discipline from two states to three: lockFieldsAbsentCount exists because absent, unreadable and readable are distinct facts about a lock, and its description tells the reader outright that a zero legalHoldOnCount over an entirely-absent population means B2 did not report, not that nothing is locked — with the cross-reference to b2/bucket's fileLockEnabled that resolves which it is. serverSideEncryption and fileInfo are held loosely (only mode is projected; a non-object fileInfo degrades to {}) so an unexpected shape cannot sink a 24-bucket scan. Field coverage is verified by execution: the mechanical harness diffs each spec's schema keys against the keys actually written and confirms 1:1 in both directions (aggregate 30/30, file 23/23), plus per-write completeness and a live safeParse of every write.

Both specs are lifetime 'infinite' with garbageCollection 50, matching b2-bucket and b2-key. That is right for aggregate, whose value is the trend — 50 versions of a per-bucket byte total is the series that shows whether the hidden-version debt is growing or being reaped, which is the whole point now that the debt is sized at 39.49 GiB. For file it is effectively moot in detailed mode: a fileId is immutable and never revisited, so each instance accumulates exactly one version and the cap never binds. The consequence is instance-count growth rather than version growth, which is inherent to per-file emission and is why detailed mode is opt-in and hard-capped by a required maxFiles.

Covers all eight operations PRD §4 assigns to this model: b2_list_file_names and b2_list_file_versions (scan), b2_get_file_info (sync/update re-read), b2_delete_file_version (delete), b2_hide_file (hide), b2_copy_file (copy), b2_update_file_legal_hold and b2_update_file_retention (update). Method names follow the PRD rather than the §3 taxonomy for hide and copy, which is a deliberate, documented divergence — see preflight-checks. Deliberately out of scope and stated as such: b2_copy_file is capped by B2 at 5 GB, and the large-file copy path belongs to @sntxrr/b2/transfer in wave 3.

TWO checks, both labelled policy: credentials-present and single-bucket-for-file-methods. A third, file-destruction-acknowledged, SHIPPED IN 2026.08.05.1 AND IS REMOVED HERE — this version exists for that removal. The check gated delete on allowFileDestruction, but swamp does not pass method inputs to checks, so it could only read globalArgs. That made --input allowFileDestruction=true — the acknowledgement its own error message told the operator to pass — invisible to it, and the run was rejected before execute ever saw the flag. Verified against the PUBLISHED version rather than reasoned about: running `swamp model method run b2-files-audit delete --input fileId=... --input allowFileDestruction=true` fails the pre-flight with a message instructing you to pass exactly what you just passed. The consequence was worse than a self-contradicting message. With the per-run path blocked, the only route to deleting anything was setting allowFileDestruction: true permanently on the model definition — so a check written to prevent accidental destruction was forcing operators to arm destruction for good, on a model whose delete can leave a restic repository unreadable with no error until the next restore. It failed on the safe configuration and passed on the dangerous one. The real gate, assertDestructionAllowed inside delete and hide, is unchanged, sees both the input and the global argument, runs before any B2 call, and additionally covers hide — which no pre-flight check could ever guard, since checks fire only for methods named create/update/delete/action. single-bucket-for-file-methods is retained and is NOT the same shape: bucketName is genuinely model configuration and has no method-input equivalent, so a check is the right place for it. Recorded in CONVENTIONS §4 item 11.

Every instance is spec-prefixed per CONVENTIONS §2, since instance names share one flat storage namespace across specs and one scan writes both. aggregate names additionally carry an FNV-1a hash of the raw (bucketName, group) pair, because a prefix group is user-controlled text containing slashes that must be sanitized to be path-safe and sanitization is lossy — 'data/' and 'data_' reduce alike and are kept distinct by the hash, asserted by test. The bucket-wide total is encoded with a sentinel that no B2 prefix can produce, making a total-versus-root-group collision structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely. file keys on fileId, never fileName, because a name has arbitrarily many versions and keying by name would make a detailed scan's versions overwrite each other. The reserved literal 'latest' is unreachable (every name is prefixed), asserted directly and re-checked by the mechanical harness, which also proves no single execution writes the same instance twice — the failure that made b2-bucket's notification snapshot eat its bucket snapshot.

Resources are shaped for CEL querying: scalar, introspectable fields rather than nested blobs, so the questions this model exists to answer are one predicate each. The README gives the two that matter — filtering on nonCurrentBytes != null && > 0 to find buckets paying for data they no longer serve, and on truncated == true to check whether that number is even complete. The live run proved both queries out: they are what located the worst offender at 20.57 GiB of non-current data against 92% waste, and what caught that the six largest buckets had silently stopped at the page cap. The nullable-metric contract is what makes those queries safe: a null cannot be mistaken for a zero by a > 0 filter, which is precisely how the wave-1 unprunedPrefixes bug hid all 24 buckets from exactly this kind of query. Authorization flags sit beside their values so a consumer can distinguish 'unlocked' from 'not allowed to look', and lockFieldsAbsentCount adds the third case — 'never reported' — so a lock-state query cannot silently read absence as safety.

Second publish. 2026.08.05.1 -> 2026.08.06.1 removes the file-destruction-acknowledged pre-flight check, and the compatibility analysis is what makes this safe to ship as a routine bump. The change can only ever turn a FAILING run into a running one: no operator could have depended on delete being blocked, because the only way to get past the check was to set allowFileDestruction permanently on the model — and that configuration still works unchanged. Anyone who applied that workaround can now drop it and acknowledge per run instead, which is a strictly better posture. No resource schema, instance name, method name or argument changed, so no snapshot is orphaned and no CEL query breaks. The forward-looking commitments from the first publish stand: nullable non-current metrics must not start reporting 0, lockFieldsAbsentCount stays three-state, file instances stay keyed by fileId, and adding an aggregate field is additive while narrowing a nullable one is not. Added to that list: no pre-flight check may be reintroduced to gate delete on the acknowledgement, and a test now enforces it.
